newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: World told to narrow divisions to attain free trade.
newsitem.headline: World told to narrow divisions to attain free trade.

text.p: A major world trade conference opened on Monday to ringing calls to avoid North-South division and to create more liberalised global commerce that would benefit the poor and make life safer for everyone.

Renato Ruggiero, director-general of the World Trade Organisation, set the tone by urging the first ministerial conference since the WTO was founded two years ago to agree on key issues despite their political sensitivity.
The Geneva-based organisation's 128 member states disagree over an Information Technology Agreement (ITA) and the question of whether labour standards should be subject to WTO rules.
Ruggiero said the draft ITA, which seeks to eliminate tariffs on an estimated $1 trillion worth of annual world trade in computer and telecommunications products, was critical.
"In the economy of the 21st Century, knowledge, like water, will be an essential resource," he said.
Deep disagreements persist over the ITA -- what it should include, how far it should go and how soon it should come into force.
The United States is pushing hard for an ITA pact this week that would cut tariffs by 2000, and Charlene Barshefsky, the Acting U.S. Trade Representative, put Washington's agenda in stark terms.

She told the conference that Washington, which accounts for 50 percent of world telecommunications revenue, "cannot and we will not settle for a situation where we are unable to operate in the other half of the world's markets".
The United States also faced opposition from some major Western nations -- and from WTO hosts Singapore -- on the divisive issue of linking trade and labour standards.
Trade ministers from Britain, Australia and Germany all said the WTO should not discuss issues such as child and slave labour.
And Singapore's Prime Minister Goh Tok Chong warned the big powers not to push the emerging economies too hard.
Developing nations see such links as a western attempt to take away their advantage of cheap labour.
"Realistically, global trade liberalisation has to progress in an incremental manner, even though some of us may prefer quantum leaps," Goh said.
In his inaugural speech, Goh set up a broader canvas for the week-long meeting. He told the trade officials that liberalisation meant more trade, more investment, more peace.

"This will mean even higher living standards of living for all. Growing economic prosperity will in turn lead to greater international security and stability. This is not fantasy, but a vision within reach," he declared.

The United States and Europe raised their voices to warn of the need for determination to narrow differences between North and South, as well as North and North, that could jeopardise the free trade goal.
The WTO meeting, which seeks to draw up a blueprint for global trade in the next century, should send a clear message to the world, Goh said.

"It should be a firm message about our determination to fight the marginalisation of people and regions, and about the power of trade to promote growth which allows governments to address problems of distribution," he said.
Goh signalled that trade in information technology products, which the WTO says outstrips world exports of agricultural products, would probably dominate the week's meetings.
"By liberalising information technologies we can educate our people on a scale unimaginable 10 or 20 years ago, empowering them to compete in the global economy," he said.
The USTR's Barshefsky said the ITA would help to put less costly technologies in the hands of businesses around the globe, making them more competitive.

"That's why we must reach agreement this week," Barshefsky told ministers. "Remaining issues are ripe for decision. We have an historic opportunity to eliminate tariffs on these products. We must seize it."

The European Union differs with Washington over just what products should be covered by the pact, arguing that it is partly designed to favour U.S. goods and does not take EU interests fully into account.
EU Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said the Singapore meeting would be judged a failure if it did not make progress on ITA.

"I should not have to say that we all have to make a further effort. But we do. If we do not make substantial progress on both issues this week, with new offers tabled, then our meeting will not be the big success we all want," he told ministers.
